_comment: Network Spell Book catalog. Pure data: no commands are ever executed from this file. 'cmd' strings are reference text shown in the UI and copied to the clipboard on request; the plugin never runs them.

categories.name: Capture & Analyze
categories.blurb: See the actual packets on the wire.

tools.what: CLI packet capture. The Linux equivalent of a SPAN session, running on your own NIC. Works over SSH and inside containers where a GUI cannot.
tools.note: -n skips name resolution. Add -w file.pcap to save for later analysis.

tools.what: Wireshark's dissection engine without the GUI. Scriptable, with the same protocol decoders.
tools.note: -f is a capture filter (BPF); -Y is a display filter (Wireshark syntax).

tools.what: Full graphical protocol analyzer. Use it to think about a capture, not to take one.
tools.note: Capture on the box with the problem; analyze on the box with a screen.

tools.what: Wireshark's interactive UI inside the terminal. The best way to read a pcap over SSH.
tools.note: Reads anything tcpdump or tshark wrote.

tools.what: grep for network traffic. Matches a regex against packet payloads.
tools.note: Only useful on unencrypted traffic.

tools.what: Replay a captured pcap back onto an interface. Reproduce a traffic pattern in a lab on demand.
tools.note: Replay into a lab, never into production.

tools.what: The authoritative DNS query tool. Ask a specific server a specific question and see the full response including flags and timing.
tools.note: +short for just the answer, +trace to follow delegation from the root.

tools.what: Quick one-line name lookup. Good enough for 'what is this A record'.
tools.note: Simpler output than dig, less detail.

tools.what: Interactive resolver query, familiar from Windows. Works fine, but dig is the Linux-native choice.
tools.note: Kept for muscle memory; prefer dig for real work.

tools.what: Modern DNS client with colorized output and DoH/DoT support built in.
tools.note: Easier to read than dig; dig is still the one on every server.

categories.name: Path & Reachability
categories.blurb: Is it up, how do we get there, and where does it break.

tools.what: Layer 3 reachability and round-trip time. The first question you ever ask.
tools.note: -c bounds the count so it exits on its own.

tools.what: Layer 2 reachability via ARP. Proves a host is on your local segment even when it ignores ICMP.
tools.note: Only works on the local broadcast domain — it does not route.

tools.what: Hop-by-hop path discovery using TTL expiry.
tools.note: -I uses ICMP, -T uses TCP when UDP probes are filtered.

tools.what: Traceroute and ping combined, updating continuously. Shows WHERE loss happens, not merely that it does.
tools.note: Loss on middle hops is usually ICMP rate-limiting. Only the final hop's loss is real.

tools.what: Modern traceroute/mtr in one TUI, with per-hop history and jitter graphs.
tools.note: Binary is named 'trip'. Same ICMP rate-limit caveat as mtr.

tools.what: Ping many hosts in parallel. Sweep a subnet for what answers.
tools.note: -a lists only alive hosts; -g takes a range or CIDR.

tools.what: Measure real throughput between two hosts with generated traffic. Turns 'the link feels slow' into a number.
tools.note: Needs a server at the far end: iperf3 -s

tools.what: NIC speed, duplex, autonegotiation and error counters. Your 'show interface' for physical detail.
tools.note: On WiFi use 'iw dev wlo1 link' instead — far more useful than ethtool there.

tools.what: LLDP/CDP neighbor discovery. Tells you which switch and which port you are plugged into, and often the VLAN.
tools.note: Needs the daemon running: sudo systemctl enable --now lldpd. It advertises you on the wire.

tools.what: Serial console client. Replaces PuTTY/minicom for console-cable work on real gear.
tools.note: Default 115200 8N1. Ctrl-t q to quit, Ctrl-t ? for help.

tools.what: The modern Linux interface, address and route command. Replaces ifconfig and route entirely.
tools.note: -br gives brief output. Also: ip -br link, ip route, ip neigh.

tools.what: Inspect and configure Linux bridges, including VLAN filtering and FDB entries.
tools.note: bridge fdb show is the Linux equivalent of 'show mac address-table'.

categories.name: Sockets & Traffic
categories.blurb: What is connected, and who is using the pipe.

tools.what: Socket statistics: listening ports, established connections, owning processes. Replaces netstat.
tools.note: t=TCP u=UDP l=listening p=process n=numeric. Needs sudo to see other users' processes.

tools.what: Live bandwidth by connection pair. Shows which conversation is consuming the link.
tools.note: Press 'n' to stop resolving names when the display churns.

tools.what: Live bandwidth grouped by process. Answers 'what on this machine is using the network'.
tools.note: The per-process view iftop does not give you.

tools.what: Terminal bandwidth monitor by process, connection and remote host at once.
tools.note: Combines the nethogs and iftop views in one screen.

tools.what: Long-term traffic accounting per interface. Answers 'how much did we move last month'.
tools.note: Needs its daemon collecting over time: systemctl enable --now vnstat.

categories.name: Discovery & Probing
categories.blurb: What is out there, and does the port answer.

tools.what: Host discovery, port scanning, service and OS fingerprinting. The standard tool for mapping a network.
tools.note: -sn is host discovery only, no port scan. Scan only networks you own or administer.

tools.what: Modern netcat: open, read and write arbitrary TCP/UDP connections. Test whether a port truly answers.
tools.note: -v verbose, -z scan without sending data.

tools.what: Arbitrary bidirectional socket plumbing: relays, port forwards, serial-to-TCP bridges.
tools.note: Enormously capable and easy to misuse. Learn it after ncat.

tools.what: Layer 2 host discovery by ARP sweep. Finds hosts that ignore ping, including their MAC vendor.
tools.note: Local segment only. Often finds devices nmap -sn misses.

tools.what: Registration lookup for a domain or IP block: owner, netblock, abuse contact.
tools.note: Identifies which provider owns an address you saw in a traceroute.

tools.what: HTTP and API client. Check headers, status codes, TLS and redirects.
tools.note: -I headers only, -v shows the full TLS handshake and request.

categories.name: Addressing Math
categories.blurb: Subnets, masks and wildcards without arithmetic errors.

tools.what: Subnet calculator with binary breakdown, showing exactly where the mask boundary falls. Excellent for learning and explaining.
tools.note: The binary column makes the mask boundary obvious at a glance.

tools.what: Terse scriptable subnet calculator with strong IPv6 support and VLSM splitting. Gives Cisco wildcard masks directly.
tools.note: Split a block: sipcalc -s 24 198.51.100.0/22

categories.name: Device Management
categories.blurb: Reaching and configuring the gear itself.

tools.what: Encrypted remote shell. Your primary access method to every device that has an IP.
tools.note: Per-host options belong in ~/.ssh/config, not in aliases.

tools.what: Walk a device's SNMP tree: interfaces, counters, uptime, inventory. Read-only monitoring data.
tools.note: Never use 'public' on a real network. Prefer SNMPv3 with auth and privacy.

tools.what: Fetch one specific SNMP OID rather than walking a whole subtree.
tools.note: Use snmptranslate to turn a numeric OID into a readable name.

tools.what: Configuration automation with vendor collections for IOS, NX-OS, EOS and JunOS. Push verified config to many devices at once.
tools.note: Bigger hammer than netmiko, steeper climb. Worth it past about ten devices.

tools.what: Routes your traffic over a plain SSH connection — a VPN without a VPN server.
tools.note: Needs only SSH access and Python on the far end.

tools.what: The current Linux firewall framework. One tool for IPv4, IPv6, ARP and bridge filtering.
tools.note: Replaces iptables. Rules live in /etc/nftables.conf.

tools.what: Simplified firewall front-end for straightforward allow/deny rules.
tools.note: Fine for a laptop; use nft directly for anything nuanced.

tools.what: The legacy packet filter. You will still meet it in older documentation and on older systems.
tools.note: Superseded by nftables. Know it for reading, write new rules in nft.

tools.what: Network simulator running real vendor images alongside containers and VMs. Build a topology and break it safely.
tools.note: Needs gns3-server running. Pairs with dynamips and docker.

tools.what: Cisco IOS emulator underneath GNS3. Runs genuine IOS images for classic routers.
tools.note: Usually driven by GNS3 rather than invoked directly.

tools.what: Containers — increasingly how network services and lab nodes are shipped and run.
tools.note: GNS3 can use containers as topology nodes.
